Thank you for this thoughtful article. As a holistic health coach and a 66-year-old woman, I often wonder what I would tell my 50-year-old self. I would tell her to worry less about being thin and focus more on nourishing her body with calcium-rich foods, adequate protein, strength-building movement, and healthy lifestyle habits.

But most importantly, I would encourage her to make an emotional shift in how she views aging.

The woman in this article who still holds on to clothes from 30 years ago really struck me. How many of us are doing the same thing, physically or emotionally? Holding on to an image of ourselves that no longer reflects who we are becoming?

Many women of my generation were raised to believe that thinness equaled beauty, desirability, and even self-worth. We have spent decades trying to control our weight, often at the expense of appreciating our bodies.

Of course, excess weight can carry health risks, but a few extra pounds as we age do not necessarily mean we are unhealthy. Perhaps it's time to shift our attention away from trying to reclaim our younger bodies and toward building strength, nourishing ourselves, and embracing the natural changes of aging.

I believe healthy aging is as much an emotional and spiritual transition as it is a physical one. What if we spent less energy trying to look like the women we were at 30 and more energy appreciating the women we are becoming?

BMI should NOT be used--it can not account for muscle weight--other measurements must be used to accurately assess a person's healthy weight.  I am 82 years old. When I was in my 20's I started gaining weight going on diets. Loosing weight and then gaining more.  So after doing this for over a year I went to see an endocrinologist  and got brilliant advice.

He said the hypothalamus that controls our appetite shuts down after 20 minutes. Most people eat quickly and finish their main entree in less then 10 minutes. The Hypothalamus  has not shut down so they still feel hungry and continue to eat more.

He said if I wanted to loose weight & keep it off, I could eat what I want & as much as I want with the PROVISO that I chew my food, eat slowly and take NO LESS than 20 minutes to eat my meal.

Eating quickly was a tough habit to change but slowing down worked!

 For almost a year I sat with a watch when I ate and made sure I did not finish in less than 20 minutes. Now its automatic.

I lost my 26 lbs and have stayed the same weight between 110 & 118 (winter adds a few lbs) for the past 50 years.  

Eating on the run and gobbling down our food in America is what everyone does & in my view contributes obesity along with not moving much.

Movement is Key!

While I could afford it (am a retired lawyer Judge) never owned a car. Walk every where and do daily Qigong. 

Sad to see that in North America people take better care of their car than their body.

I think you have it wrong here. The fiancée’s has an interest in knowing the truth, but the Ethicist overlooks the ethical responsibility of the person conveying the information.

There are two separate ethical questions here:
* Does the fiancée deserve to know? If true, probably yes. She should have an opportunity to make an informed decision before marrying.
* Who should tell her? That’s where I disagree with the Ethicist.

The woman in the relationship has firsthand knowledge. She can explain what happened, when it happened, and what she knew about the man’s relationship status. She may also have text messages or other evidence supporting her account.

The letter writer, by contrast, has no personal knowledge of the alleged infidelity. He/She would be repeating someone else’s account to a woman he/she barely knows.

That’s hearsay even if the information happens to be true. And while hearsay isn’t necessarily false, it carries obvious risks of misunderstanding, misinterpretation, exaggeration, incomplete context, and possibly later denial by the source of its accuracy.

There’s another problem: The Ethicist effectively allows the person with firsthand knowledge to avoid the uncomfortable consequences of disclosure while encouraging a third party to assume that burden. That strikes me as ethically inconsistent.

If the friend believes strongly enough that the fiancée deserves to know, she should be willing to take responsibility for communicating what she personally knows.

 Duty of Loyalty: Executives and board members must put the company’s interests above their own personal, financial, or romantic interests. Engaging in undisclosed relationships with business counterparties (like Alice Huang at Megaspeed) or subordinates creates severe conflicts of interest, exposes the company to blackmail or regulatory penalties, and violates this duty. 

Duty of Care: Leaders must make informed, prudent decisions and maintain reasonable oversight to protect company assets and value. When a CEO's personal conduct triggers federal investigations, national security scrutiny, or reputational damage that threatens shareholder value, the board of directors has a fiduciary duty to investigate and, if necessary, remove the executive to protect the company.

comments.body: Being an avid hiker here in the Pacific NW, I have had many, many encounters with Black Bears, which are generally (but not always!) quite shy. I did some hiking in the Canadian Rockies back in my college days, and had one close encounter in Yoho Park with an immature Grizzly: me, hiking down a series of switchbacks, and the bear hiking up. The bear apparently hadn't caught my scent, and they have pretty limited eyesight, so I caught sight of the bear first, and just stood still; the bear didn't realize I was there until it turned the corner on the switchback and was directly facing me from maybe 5 yards. By then I was shaking in my boots! The bear let out an explosive breathy "whoosh" sound and made a beeline straight up the hillside. I dropped off the trail and gave it a very wide berth. It was somewhat amusing to see the bear peering down through the brush as I made my getaway. Much respect! Maybe even mutual.

I was astonished to learn there that about 30% of the Operating cost of such technologies was the expected Environmental assessment cost (and ~4% of the Capital cost).  This seemed pretty high, to me, for technologies that were called into being by an effort, essentially, to save the environment from the effects of Global Warming.  This seemed excessive and raises the price of the electricity produced by these MEC technologies out-of-bounds compared to competing technologies.  It would seem that full environmental assessment of one WEC off the California coast would suffice enough to lower the assessment required of further WEC's on that coastline.  This may be an example of how you drown good ideas in bureaucratic red ink.  Engineers evaluate the costing of these ideas using the costs expected of them, and abandon those ideas the moment they appear cost-ineffective.

Born in July 1951, I am very much my parents' child. However, both coming of age towards the end of the Depression and both civilian employees of the U.S. Army Signal Corps (how they met in late 1943 over a telephone call), they raised me as a child of the 1940s. 

The events you cite from your birth date's Times are events I learned orally from my parents, in classrooms and textbooks, in independent reading, and from the excellent, fact-based documentaries required of our broadcasting networks.

Where I differ from you is the value of coincidences. As my life winds down and my time past exceeds expectations of the future, I DO look at the coincidences in my life as I sum things up at 75. Tears of mourning of those I lost have become tears of remembrance and gratitude for having known them and by that time together we have formed each others' characters.

comments.name: Dr Socrates
comments.body: I was reminded of the rise and fall of Rome while reading Yee's fascinating piece, what with all of the time and resources Ms. DeKreek has to pour into her own image, similar to wealthy Roman women thousands of years ago. In Satire 6, 350 years before Rome's fall, Juvenal writes, "[A Roman woman of the elite] presents a sight as funny as it's appalling, her features lost under a damp bread face-pack...". A hundred years later, Tertullian writes that "the force of the cosmetics burns ruin into the hair; and the constant application of even any undrugged moisture, lays up a store of harm for the head...". I think we live in a similar age and have a similar distance to our own cultural end; this article is yet another marker suggesting that we are surely on that path.

comments.name: Tim Barrus
comments.body: Great book. Great review. The review itself crackles with insight. I often wonder why it is that we have this wild cultural romance with difficult characters who are as marginal as they are enigmatic. Books are too expensive, and then after you crack the book, there's no there there. American fiction feels like I am struggling to hold a wet glob of cement in my hands. But not this book. Riverhead is having quite a year with the Disappearancers and Stations. My own policy is to always name who the real publisher is. Random House owns Riverhead. In a hundred thousand million billion years, Random House will not be arriving like a boombox carried defiantly through the underground railway. Random House will arrive with cold corporate indifference. They have to actually create a seperate company (Riverhead) to market a book Random House cannot sell because the brand is the icon of a suit. Random House Publishing Group is owned by Penguin Random House, which is wholly owned by the German media conglomerate Bertelsmann. I published two books with these publishers. It was a cold, corporate, indifferent experience. I am sorry I did it. It was a mistake. It was not a fit. It just leaves a bad taste in your mouth, and you walk away. So these publishing companies build imprints which theoretically imbues them with a more accessible sense of humanity. It never works. You can dress it up, but it's still Random House. Great book. It sings.     The characters drive the story with a whip.

“If you’re mad at the system, I’m sorry,” she said. “But you don’t get a book deal because you deserve it.”

This is the hard edged advice or truth telling that a lot of people need to hear and internalize. Publishing is a business and it is intensely subjective. That is simply the way it is and aspiring authors must take it to heart and figure out how their manuscript solves and agent and publisher's problem: is it a great story well told and will the author be able to sell it.

That said, publishing still relies too heavily on things like social media followers to determine if a book has a market. The connection between social media platform and sales is tenuous at best, so it is on agents and publishers to come up with a more sophisticated measure.
